title: Physics — Unit 2 Forces of Earth (targets 2.1-2.3)
source: Carter's three learning-target pages for Unit 2. Sets rotate: the dashboard sends Set: N on every new drill. Set 4 is force diagrams plus repair of the items missed on 2026-11-15; set 5 is quantitative and level-4 extension. Every option in an item carries the same word count so length cannot hint at the key.

questions.stem: A cross-section model has to show which layer is liquid. Which claim is correct, and what is the evidence?
options: Outer core; shear waves stop at this boundary
Mantle; it flows slowly under the rigid plates
Inner core; it is hotter than layers above
Crust; it bends plastically beneath the deep oceans
questions.why: Only the outer core is liquid, and S-waves cannot travel through a liquid, which is the seismic evidence.

questions.stem: The inner core is hotter than the outer core, yet it is solid. Why?
options: Iron becomes solid as it loses radiogenic heat
Pressure at that depth raises the melting point
Inner core is actually cooler than the mantle
Convection in the core removes heat very quickly
questions.why: Melting point rises with pressure, so the deepest iron stays solid despite a temperature above the outer core's.

questions.stem: A student writes that the mantle is molten rock. Which correction is right?
options: The mantle is liquid only beneath the deep oceans
The mantle is solid and never deforms at all
The mantle is solid rock that flows over time
The mantle is a gas at those asthenosphere depths
questions.why: The mantle is solid; it deforms plastically over geologic time, and only the outer core is liquid.

questions.stem: Where inside Earth do nuclear processes occur, and which process is it?
options: Crust only; fusion of hydrogen into helium gas
Core only; fusion of iron into heavier nuclei
Mantle only; fission of silicate minerals into oxides
Core and mantle; radioactive decay of heavy isotopes
questions.why: Long-lived isotopes such as U-238, U-235, Th-232 and K-40 decay in the core and mantle; fusion is a stellar process.

questions.stem: How does one radioactive decay event deliver heat to the surrounding rock?
options: Emitted particles and gamma rays are absorbed
The nucleus releases chemical bonds that burn
Friction between decaying atoms generates the heat
Magnetic reconnection converts each decay into photons
questions.why: Decay energy leaves as particle kinetic energy and gamma radiation, which the surrounding rock absorbs and thermalizes.

questions.stem: Which pair correctly distinguishes the two sources of Earth's internal heat?
options: Primordial is continuous; radiogenic is leftover heat
Primordial is leftover; radiogenic is produced continuously
Primordial is solar; radiogenic comes from friction
Primordial is tidal; radiogenic comes from pressure
questions.why: Primordial heat is accretional heat still draining out; radiogenic heat is generated now by radioactive decay.

questions.stem: If radiogenic heating declined sharply, what would happen to plate motion?
options: Convection would strengthen and plates would speed
Convection would reverse and plates would stop
Convection would weaken and plates would slow
Convection stops although plates continue moving quickly
questions.why: Decay heat sustains convection; less heat means weaker convection, less slab pull, and slower plates.

questions.stem: Why does hot mantle material rise in a convection cell?
options: It is pushed upward by the overriding plate above
It is denser than the material beneath the crust
It is pulled upward by the nearby sinking slab
It is less dense than the surrounding cooler rock
questions.why: Rising material is buoyant because it is less dense; nothing needs to push it up.

questions.stem: On a force vector diagram of a plate, which arrow should be drawn largest?
options: Slab pull at the subducting end, pointing downward
Ridge push at the spreading end, pointing outward
Friction along the plate base, opposing its motion
Mantle drag along the base, following the flow
questions.why: Slab pull is the dominant plate force, so its vector should be longest and labeled.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly connects convection to a force acting on a plate?
options: Rising hot rock pushes the plate away from ridges
Sinking cool rock drags the plate toward the trench
Spreading ridges pull the plate toward the nearby continent
Mantle drag pushes the plate upward into the crust
questions.why: The descending limb drags lithosphere down and inward, which is the mechanism behind slab pull.

questions.stem: At a divergent boundary in an ocean basin, which feature forms?
options: A deep trench with deep earthquakes and island arcs
A strike-slip fault with shallow quakes and no magma
A mid-ocean ridge with shallow earthquakes and active volcanism
A folded mountain belt made of thickened continental crust
questions.why: Divergence creates new oceanic crust at a ridge, with shallow quakes and decompression melting.

questions.stem: An oceanic plate meets a continental plate. What forms, and why?
options: Folded mountains and no trench, because neither plate subducts
A ridge and rift valley, because plates move apart
A transform fault, because the plates slide past sideways
Trench and volcanic arc, because the oceanic plate subducts
questions.why: Oceanic lithosphere is denser, so it subducts, producing a trench and a volcanic arc above the slab.

questions.stem: Two continental plates collide. What is the result?
options: A folded mountain belt with thickened crust, no trench
A trench with deep earthquakes and explosive arc volcanoes
A mid-ocean ridge with new crust and shallow quakes
A transform fault with offset streams and no volcanism
questions.why: Continental crust is too buoyant to subduct, so the plates shorten and thicken into a mountain belt.

questions.stem: Which set of features belongs to a transform boundary?
options: Deep earthquakes, island arcs, and explosive volcanism
Shallow earthquakes, offset stream channels, no volcanism
Shallow earthquakes, new oceanic crust, and ridges
Intermediate earthquakes, folded rock, and thick crust
questions.why: Transform motion is strike-slip: shallow quakes, offset features, and no magma because nothing rises or sinks.

questions.stem: Earthquake depth increases with distance from a trench. What does that show?
options: Quakes follow the hot mantle as it rises
Quakes follow the ridge as new crust forms
Quakes follow the cold slab as it sinks
Quakes follow the fault as plates slide sideways
questions.why: The Benioff zone tracks the dipping slab, which is why deep quakes occur only at subduction zones.

questions.stem: Why does a transform boundary produce no volcanoes?
options: Magma forms there but cannot reach the surface very quickly
The crust is too thin to hold a magma chamber
The plates there move too slowly to generate any heat
No material rises or subducts there, so nothing ever melts
questions.why: Melting needs decompression or added water; transform motion supplies neither, so no magma is generated.

questions.stem: Magnetic striping on the seafloor is symmetric about a ridge. What does it prove?
options: New crust records field reversals as it spreads outward
Old crust is folded by compression at the ridge
The ridge moves sideways across a stationary ocean floor
Deep sediment layers align with the present magnetic field
questions.why: Basalt records the field as it cools, and the mirrored pattern on both sides shows crust moving away from the ridge.

questions.stem: Ocean crust is nowhere older than about 200 million years. Why?
options: Ocean crust forms too slowly to accumulate older rock
Ocean crust is recycled into trenches at subduction zones
The ocean crust is continually melted by ridge volcanism
Ocean crust is buried by sediment before aging further
questions.why: Oceanic lithosphere is destroyed at subduction zones, so the oldest seafloor is far younger than the continents.

questions.stem: Heat flow is high at a ridge and low far from it. What explains the pattern?
options: Old crust far from the ridge is heating up
Friction at the ridge generates heat along the fault
New crust near the ridge is hot and cooling
Thick sediment insulates the crust far from the ridge
questions.why: Crust cools and thickens with distance from the ridge, so heat flow falls as the lithosphere ages.

questions.stem: A GPS station moves 4 cm per year. How far does it travel in 25 million years?
options: 100 km, since 4 cm per year is 4 km per million
10,000 km, since 4 cm per year is 400 km per million
400 km, since 4 cm per year is 16 km per million
1,000 km, since 4 cm per year is 40 km per million
questions.why: 1 cm/yr equals 10 km per million years, so 4 cm/yr gives 40 km/My and 25 My gives 1,000 km.

questions.stem: How is a half-life defined for a radioactive isotope?
options: The time for half the parent atoms to decay
The time for all parent atoms to decay completely
The time for half the daughter atoms to escape
The time for the isotope to change its temperature
questions.why: A half-life is the interval in which half of the remaining parent decays, and it is constant for that isotope.

questions.stem: What fraction of the original parent remains after four half-lives?
options: 25 percent, because the parent halves only twice
6.25 percent, because the parent halves four times
12.5 percent, because the parent halves three times
3.125 percent, because the parent halves five times
questions.why: Each half-life halves the parent: 50, 25, 12.5, then 6.25 percent after four.

questions.stem: A sample holds 12.5 percent of its original parent isotope. How many half-lives have passed?
options: Two, because the parent halved two separate times
Four, because the parent halved four separate times
Three, because the parent halved three separate times
Five, because the parent halved five separate times
questions.why: 100 to 50 to 25 to 12.5 percent is three halvings, so n = 3.

questions.stem: A rock holds 12.5 percent parent and the isotope has a 700-million-year half-life. What is its age?
options: 1.4 billion years, because two half-lives have passed
2.8 billion years, because four half-lives have passed
700 million years, because one half-life has passed
2.1 billion years, because three half-lives have passed
questions.why: n = 3 and each half-life is 700 My, so age = 3 x 700 My = 2.1 billion years.

questions.stem: A sample shows a parent-to-daughter ratio of 1:3. How many half-lives have passed?
options: Two, because 75 percent of the parent has decayed
One, because 50 percent of the parent has decayed
Three, because 87.5 percent of the parent has decayed
Four, because 93.75 percent of the parent has decayed
questions.why: Daughter at 75 percent means parent at 25 percent, which is two halvings.

questions.stem: Why is carbon-14 unsuitable for dating a 70-million-year-old rock?
options: Its 1.25-billion-year half-life leaves too little daughter
Its 5,730-year half-life leaves too little parent
Its 4.5-billion-year half-life leaves too little parent
Its 48.8-billion-year half-life leaves too little daughter
questions.why: Beyond about ten half-lives the remaining parent is unmeasurable, and C-14 also dates only once-living material.

questions.stem: Which isotope would you use to date a volcanic ash layer, and why?
options: Carbon-14, because its half-life suits million-year rock
Uranium-238, because its half-life suits thousand-year bone
Potassium-40, because its half-life suits million-year rock
Rubidium-87, because its half-life suits thousand-year shell
questions.why: K-40 has a half-life near 1.25 billion years and is built into volcanic minerals, so it dates the eruption.

questions.stem: Which difference between relative and absolute dating is stated correctly?
options: Relative gives years; absolute gives only the relative order
Relative uses the radioactive isotopes; absolute uses rock superposition
Relative dates single minerals; absolute dates whole rock units
Relative gives order; absolute gives an age in years
questions.why: Relative dating orders events using superposition and cross-cutting; absolute dating converts a ratio into years.

questions.stem: A fault cuts through three sedimentary layers. What can you conclude?
options: The fault is younger than the layers it cuts
The fault is older than the layers it cuts
Fault is the same age as the lowest layer
The fault is older than the folded rock intrusion
questions.why: Cross-cutting relationships: a feature that cuts another must be younger than what it cuts.

questions.stem: How would you find the absolute age of a fossil between two ash layers?
options: Date the fossil bone itself directly with uranium-lead isotopes
Date both ash layers, bracketing the fossil between them
Date the sedimentary rock grains surrounding the whole fossil
Date the lowest layer in the exposed cliff section
questions.why: Volcanic ash is datable and bounds the fossil in time, which is why ash layers are the standard bracket.

questions.stem: Why does constant radioactive decay let geologists read a rock's age?
options: The decay rate slows predictably as the rock gets older
The daughter isotope leaks out at a measurable constant rate
The parent-to-daughter ratio in the closed mineral records elapsed half-lives
The parent isotope is replenished at a constant known rate
questions.why: Because the decay rate does not change, the ratio in a closed mineral is a clock that records elapsed time.

questions.stem: Which condition must hold for a radiometric date to be trustworthy?
options: The whole rock was metamorphosed after the mineral had formed
The rock sample contains several different radioactive isotopes of uranium
The mineral was heated well above its melting point later
The mineral stayed closed, losing no parent or daughter atoms
questions.why: An open system loses or gains parent or daughter and the ratio no longer records the original age.

questions.stem: A rock gives an age of 1.4 billion years with a 700-million-year isotope. What fraction of parent remains?
options: 25 percent, because two half-lives have elapsed
50 percent, because one half-life has elapsed
12.5 percent, because three half-lives have elapsed
6.25 percent, because four half-lives have elapsed
questions.why: 1.4 billion divided by 700 million is n = 2, so the parent has halved twice to 25 percent.

questions.stem: A GPS station moves 4 cm per year. How far does it travel in 25 million years?
options: 100 km, since 4 cm per year is 4 km per million
10,000 km, since 4 cm per year is 400 km per million
400 km, since 4 cm per year is 16 km per million
1,000 km, since 4 cm per year is 40 km per million
questions.why: 1 cm/yr equals 10 km per million years, so 4 cm/yr gives 40 km/My and 25 My gives 1,000 km.

The time for all parent atoms to decay completely

6.25 percent, because the parent halves four times
12.5 percent, because the parent halves three times
3.125 percent, because the parent halves five times
questions.why: Each half-life halves the parent: 50, 25, 12.5, then 6.25 percent after four.

Four, because the parent halved four separate times
Three, because the parent halved three separate times
Five, because the parent halved five separate times

Relative dates single minerals; absolute dates whole rock units
Relative gives order; absolute gives an age in years
questions.why: Relative dating orders events using superposition and cross-cutting; absolute dating converts a ratio into years.

questions.stem: A fault cuts through three sedimentary layers. What can you conclude?
options: The fault is younger than the layers it cuts
The fault is older than the layers it cuts
Fault is the same age as the lowest layer
The fault is older than the folded rock intrusion
questions.why: Cross-cutting relationships: a feature that cuts another must be younger than what it cuts.

questions.stem: How would you find the absolute age of a fossil between two ash layers?
options: Date the fossil bone itself directly with uranium-lead isotopes
Date both ash layers, bracketing the fossil between them
Date the sedimentary rock grains surrounding the whole fossil
Date the lowest layer in the exposed cliff section
questions.why: Volcanic ash is datable and bounds the fossil in time, which is why ash layers are the standard bracket.

6.25 percent, because four half-lives have elapsed
questions.why: 1.4 billion divided by 700 million is n = 2, so the parent has halved twice to 25 percent.

questions.stem: Oceanic crust and continental crust differ in thickness and density. Which comparison is correct?
options: Oceanic is thinner and denser than continental crust
Oceanic is thicker and denser than continental crust
Oceanic is thinner and lighter than continental crust
Oceanic is thicker and lighter than continental crust
questions.why: Oceanic crust is about 7 km of basalt; continental crust is thicker granite, which is less dense.

questions.stem: Which layer accounts for the greatest share of Earth's volume?
options: The crust, a thin shell of basaltic ocean floor
The mantle, a thick shell of flowing silicate rock
The outer core, a layer of liquid iron alloy
The inner core, a sphere of solid iron alloy
questions.why: The mantle extends roughly 2,900 km and holds most of Earth's volume and mass.

questions.stem: Why does the asthenosphere flow while the lithosphere above it does not?
options: It is made of liquid iron rather than silicate rock
It is under much less pressure than the crust above
It sits closer to its melting point at that depth
It contains no radioactive isotopes to warm it at all
questions.why: Higher temperature at depth brings rock near its melting point, so it deforms plastically over time.

questions.stem: Which isotope is a major source of Earth's radiogenic heat?
options: Carbon-14, decaying quickly inside the shallow crust
Hydrogen-1, fusing slowly inside the inner core
Iron-56, splitting rapidly inside the outer core
Potassium-40, decaying slowly inside the mantle
questions.why: K-40, U-238, U-235 and Th-232 are the long-lived heat-producing isotopes in the mantle and core.

questions.stem: Heat production per kilogram of rock from radioactive decay is best described as what?
options: Nearly constant over the isotope's decay timescale
Increasing sharply as the rock gets older
Dropping to zero after one single half-life
Dependent on pressure rather than on the isotope
questions.why: Decay rate is fixed per isotope, so heat per kilogram stays steady until the isotope is depleted.

questions.stem: Which long-term change follows if Earth's radiogenic heat production falls?
options: Convection strengthens and plate motion speeds up instead
Convection weakens and plate motion slows over time
Convection reverses direction and plates then move inland
Convection stops and the plates freeze in place
questions.why: Less heat means weaker convection, less slab pull, and slower plates — a long-term, not instant, change.

questions.stem: On a plate diagram, the arrow pulling the subducting slab downward represents what?
options: Ridge push, the weakest force acting on the plate
Mantle drag, the force pushing plates apart sideways
Slab pull, the dominant force driving plate motion
Friction, the force that accelerates the descending slab
questions.why: The cold dense slab sinks under its own weight; slab pull is the largest plate-driving force.

questions.stem: What produces ridge push at a mid-ocean ridge?
options: Hot mantle pushes sideways against the ridge axis
Subducting slabs drag the plate toward the ridge
Friction between plates pulls crust into the ridge
Elevated lithosphere slides downslope away from the ridge
questions.why: The ridge stands high, so lithosphere slides away from it under gravity — a smaller force than slab pull.

questions.stem: In a force diagram, what does the friction arrow along a plate's base do?
options: Opposes the plate's motion, thus reducing its speed
Adds to slab pull, increasing the plate's speed
Pushes the plate sideways toward the ridge axis
Has no effect, since friction cannot act on rock
questions.why: Friction and mantle drag resist motion, so they point opposite the plate's direction of travel.

questions.stem: In a mantle convection cell, where does the descending limb typically lie?
options: Above a mid-ocean ridge, where hot rock rises
Above a subduction zone, where cold rock sinks
Directly beneath a continental interior, where rock is hottest
Along a transform fault, where plates slide sideways
questions.why: Cooled lithosphere sinks at convergent margins, which is why descending limbs line up with subduction zones.

questions.stem: Continental crust pulls apart at a divergent boundary. Which feature forms?
options: A deep trench with a long volcanic island chain
A folded mountain belt built from greatly thickened crust
A rift valley with normal faults and thinning crust
A strike-slip fault with clearly offset rock layers
questions.why: Continental rifting produces a valley bounded by normal faults, as in the East African Rift.

questions.stem: Two oceanic plates converge. Which pair of features forms?
options: A rift valley with a chain of hot volcanoes
A folded mountain belt and a broad plateau
A long transform fault with offset stream channels
A deep trench and a volcanic island arc
questions.why: One oceanic plate subducts, creating a trench and an arc of volcanoes above the slab.

questions.stem: Which boundary is the classic example of transform motion?
options: The San Andreas fault, where plates slide past
The Mid-Atlantic Ridge, where new crust forms
The Andes, where oceanic crust subducts inland
The East African Rift, where a continent splits
questions.why: The San Andreas is a strike-slip boundary: two plates slide horizontally past each other.

questions.stem: Which feature is never produced at a transform boundary?
options: Shallow earthquakes from sudden slip along a fault
New oceanic crust created by upwelling magma
Offset streams and roads cut by lateral motion
Fractured rock along a linear fault trace
questions.why: Transform motion neither creates nor destroys crust and generates no magma.

questions.stem: Which boundary type creates new lithosphere?
options: Transform, where plates slide horizontally past each other
Convergent, where one plate descends into the mantle
Divergent, where upwelling magma forms new ocean crust
Collisional, where two continents weld together into one
questions.why: Only divergence adds new crust; convergence destroys it and transform neither.

questions.stem: Which observation is the strongest direct evidence for subduction?
options: Shallow earthquakes scattered across a continent interior
Volcanoes erupting at the center of a plate
Magnetic stripes running parallel to a coastline
Earthquake depth increasing inland from a trench
questions.why: Deep quakes only occur inside a descending slab, so the depth trend traces subduction in data.

questions.stem: What creates the magnetic striping pattern on the seafloor?
options: Basalt cooling during reversals of Earth's field
Sediment layers sorting themselves by grain size
Glaciers depositing magnetic minerals in stripes
Magma chambers aligning with the current field
questions.why: New basalt records the field direction when it cools, so reversals leave mirrored stripes.

questions.stem: Where is the oldest ocean crust found?
options: At the ridge axis, where crust is newest
Farthest from the ridge, near subduction zones
In the middle of a wide ocean basin
Beneath continental shelves, close to the shoreline
questions.why: Crust ages as it moves away from the ridge, so the oldest seafloor lies near trenches.

questions.stem: GPS vectors on either side of a mid-ocean ridge point where?
options: Toward the ridge axis, from both sides equally
Parallel to the ridge, in the same direction
Away from the ridge axis, on both sides
Downward, into the asthenosphere that lies below them
questions.why: Divergent motion means the two plates move apart, so both vectors point away from the ridge.

questions.stem: Where would you expect the highest heat flow?
options: In the center of an old deep ocean basin
Along a transform fault far from any spreading ridge
Beneath a thick continental mountain belt like the Andes
At a mid-ocean ridge, where new crust is hot
questions.why: Young crust near a ridge is still hot, so heat flow is highest there and falls with age.

questions.stem: A plate moves 3 cm per year. How far does it travel in 20 million years?
options: 600 km, since 3 cm per year is 30 km per million
60 km, since 3 cm per year is 3 km per million
6,000 km, since 3 cm per year is 300 km per million
1,200 km, since 3 cm per year is 60 km per million
questions.why: 1 cm/yr is 10 km/My, so 3 cm/yr gives 30 km/My and 20 My gives 600 km.

questions.stem: After two half-lives, what fraction of the parent isotope remains?
options: 50 percent, because the parent halved once
25 percent, because the parent halved twice
12.5 percent, because the parent halved three times
6.25 percent, because the parent halved four times
questions.why: Each half-life halves the remainder: 100 to 50 to 25 percent.

questions.stem: A rock is 1.5 billion years old and the isotope has a 500-million-year half-life. What remains?
options: 25 percent parent, after two half-lives
50 percent parent, after one half-life
12.5 percent parent, after three half-lives
6.25 percent parent, after four half-lives
questions.why: 1.5 billion divided by 500 million is n = 3, and three halvings leave 12.5 percent.

questions.stem: A sample has a parent-to-daughter ratio of 1:7. How many half-lives have passed?
options: Two, because 75 percent has decayed away
One, because 50 percent has decayed away
Four, because 93.75 percent has decayed away
Three, because 87.5 percent has decayed away
questions.why: Daughter at 87.5 percent means parent at 12.5 percent, which is three halvings.

questions.stem: Carbon-14 dating becomes unreliable after roughly how long?
options: About 50,000 years, or nine half-lives
About 5,000 years, or one half-life
About 500,000 years, or ninety half-lives
About 5 million years, ninety half-lives
questions.why: Past about ten half-lives too little parent remains to measure, and 5,730 years times ten is ~57,000.

questions.stem: A fossil lies between two volcanic ash layers. How is its age determined?
options: Date the fossil bone itself using potassium-argon
Date both ash layers and bracket the fossil
Date the sedimentary grains surrounding the fossil
Date the deepest layer in the exposed cliff
questions.why: Ash is datable and bounds the fossil in time, giving a reliable range.

questions.stem: Which material is best dated with uranium-lead?
options: A wooden tool from a young archaeological site
A shell from a shallow marine deposit
A zircon crystal from very old continental rock
A bone fragment from a recent cave deposit
questions.why: U-238's 4.5-billion-year half-life suits ancient zircons; C-14 suits young organic material.

questions.stem: Which principle places the oldest sedimentary layer at the bottom?
options: Cross-cutting, valid where faults cut layers
Original horizontality, valid for tilted beds
Faunal succession, valid for correlated fossils
Superposition, valid in undisturbed sequences
questions.why: Superposition states that undisturbed layers stack youngest on top, oldest at the base.

questions.stem: A rock contains a fragment of an older rock. What can you conclude?
options: The fragment is older than the rock containing it
The fragment is younger than the rock containing it
The fragment and host rock are the same age
The fragment formed after the host was folded
questions.why: The inclusion principle: a clast must exist before the rock that incorporates it.

questions.stem: What does an unconformity represent in a rock sequence?
options: A long period when magma intruded between the layers
A gap in time where erosion or non-deposition occurred
A fault that displaced the layers sideways over time
A fold that overturned the entire sequence of beds
questions.why: An unconformity is missing time: material was eroded or never deposited before the next layer formed.

questions.stem: Why is a closed system required for a radiometric date?
options: Pressure changes the isotope's half-life value
Heat changes the isotope's half-life value
Leaking parent or daughter changes the ratio
Water adds new radioactive parent atoms
questions.why: The ratio is the clock, so gain or loss of either isotope invalidates the age.

questions.stem: A rock holds one-eighth of its original parent isotope. If the half-life is 250 million years, how old is it?
options: 500 million years, since two half-lives passed
250 million years, since one half-life passed
1,000 million years, since four half-lives passed
750 million years, since three half-lives passed
questions.why: One-eighth remaining means n = 3, and 3 x 250 My = 750 My.

questions.stem: Which measurement would best test the seafloor spreading hypothesis?
options: Crust age plotted against distance from a ridge
Sediment color plotted against water depth offshore
Volcano height plotted against distance from a coast
Earthquake count plotted against local population density
questions.why: Spreading predicts age increasing with distance from the ridge, which is exactly what is observed.

questions.stem: S-waves from an earthquake are missing beyond a certain distance. What does that reveal?
options: A liquid layer, the outer core, blocks shear waves
A solid layer, the mantle, bends shear waves sharply
A vacuum layer, the asthenosphere, absorbs shear waves
A dense layer, the crust, reflects shear waves backward
questions.why: Shear waves cannot pass through liquid, so their shadow zone is the evidence that the outer core is liquid.

questions.stem: Which layer's slow flow drags the lithospheric plates along?
options: The inner core, which rotates faster than the mantle
The asthenosphere, which deforms plastically over geologic time
The continental crust, which spreads under its own weight
The outer core, which flows as a liquid metal
questions.why: Plates ride on the weak asthenosphere; its convection supplies mantle drag as well as slab pull.

questions.stem: How can solid mantle rock convect at all?
options: It melts completely at even the shallow mantle depths
It is a gas under the pressures of the mantle
It deforms slowly enough to flow over geologic time
It is a liquid that flows quickly like water
questions.why: Solid rock at high temperature deforms plastically, flowing centimeters per year over millions of years.

questions.stem: A plate moves at a constant speed. What must be true of the forces on it?
options: Driving forces are far larger than all resistance
Resisting forces are larger than the driving force
The plate experiences no forces of either kind
Driving forces balance all of the resisting forces
questions.why: Constant velocity means net force is zero, so slab pull and ridge push are matched by friction and drag.

questions.stem: One arrow in a plate diagram is unlabeled and points against motion. Which force is it?
options: Friction, which resists movement along the base
Slab pull, which accelerates the plate downward
Ridge push, which drives the plate outward
Mantle drag, which always assists plate motion
questions.why: The opposing arrow is resistance: friction along the base and at the boundary.

questions.stem: Which energy conversion happens during radioactive decay in the mantle?
options: Thermal energy becomes nuclear potential energy
Nuclear potential energy becomes thermal energy
Mechanical energy becomes chemical bond energy
Chemical energy becomes gravitational potential energy
questions.why: Decay converts nuclear energy into particle kinetic energy and gamma rays, which thermalize as heat.

questions.stem: Why has Earth's interior stayed hot for billions of years?
options: The Sun heats the interior directly through the crust
Friction from tides generates most of the interior heat
The mantle insulates it while decay keeps adding heat
The core stopped cooling once the crust solidified
questions.why: Slow heat loss through a thick insulating mantle plus ongoing decay keeps the interior hot.

questions.stem: A boundary shows only shallow earthquakes, offset rock units, and no volcanoes. Which type is it?
options: Convergent, where one plate descends beneath another
Divergent, where upwelling magma creates new crust
Collisional, where two continental plates weld together
Transform, where plates slide horizontally past one another
questions.why: Shallow quakes plus offset units and no magma is the transform signature.

questions.stem: A boundary shows a deep trench and earthquakes down to 600 km. Which type is it?
options: Convergent, with a slab descending into the mantle
Divergent, with new crust forming at a ridge axis
Transform, with plates sliding laterally past each other
Intraplate, with a hot spot beneath the crust
questions.why: Deep quakes require a descending slab, so the depth range identifies subduction.

questions.stem: A boundary shows a ridge axis, high heat flow, and shallow quakes. Which type is it?
options: Convergent, where crust is destroyed at a trench
Divergent, where plates move apart and magma rises
Transform, where plates slide past without new crust
Collisional, where two continents thicken the crust
questions.why: High heat flow and shallow quakes at a ridge are the divergent signature.

questions.stem: Two continents continue colliding for 50 million years. What should result?
options: A trench with a chain of island arcs
A wider ocean basin with new oceanic crust
A taller, broader mountain belt with thickened crust
A transform fault with offset river channels nearby
questions.why: Continued collision shortens and thickens crust, raising and widening the mountain belt.

questions.stem: Magnetic stripes 100 km from a ridge record an age of 5 million years. What is the spreading rate?
options: 1 cm per year, since 100 km in 5 million years
4 cm per year, since 100 km in 5 million years
10 cm per year, since 100 km in 5 million years
2 cm per year, since 100 km in 5 million years
questions.why: 100 km over 5 My is 20 km/My, and since 1 cm/yr is 10 km/My that is 2 cm/yr.

questions.stem: Which observation best distinguishes a trench from a ridge?
options: Crust at the trench is older and being destroyed
Crust at the trench is younger and being created
Crust at the trench is hotter and still cooling
Crust at the trench is thinner and newly formed
questions.why: Trenches consume old cold crust; ridges create young hot crust, so age and heat separate them.

questions.stem: Why does oceanic lithosphere subduct while continental lithosphere usually does not?
options: Continental lithosphere is much denser than the oceanic type
Old oceanic lithosphere is denser than the mantle below
Oceanic lithosphere is much thicker than the continental lithosphere
Continental lithosphere is much colder than the oceanic lithosphere
questions.why: Cold, old oceanic lithosphere is dense enough to sink; continental crust is buoyant and resists subduction.

questions.stem: Why do plates with long subducting boundaries tend to move fastest?
options: A longer slab increases friction along the plate base
A longer slab raises ridge push from the spreading center
A longer slab exerts more slab pull on the plate
A longer slab removes mantle drag from the plate
questions.why: Slab pull scales with the length of the descending slab, so plates with more subduction move faster.

questions.stem: On a decay graph, what does each halving of the parent curve mark?
options: Two half-lives on the horizontal time axis
One full decay of the daughter isotope
The start of a new mineral crystallization
One half-life on the horizontal time axis
questions.why: The parent curve is exponential, so every halving of its value is one half-life.

questions.stem: Which isotope would date a 4.4-billion-year-old zircon?
options: Uranium-238, whose half-life suits ancient crystals
Carbon-14, whose half-life suits ancient crystals
Potassium-40, whose half-life is far too short
Nitrogen-14, whose half-life suits organic remains
questions.why: U-238's 4.5-billion-year half-life matches the age, so measurable parent and daughter remain.

questions.stem: A mineral is later heated enough to lose its daughter isotope. What happens to its date?
options: The measured age becomes older than the true age
The measured age becomes younger than the true age
The measured age stays exactly the same as before
The measured age becomes impossible to interpret at all
questions.why: Losing daughter resets the ratio, so the mineral records the later heating event.

questions.stem: A fossil sits between ash dated 70 Ma and ash dated 66 Ma. What is its age?
options: Exactly 68 million years old in every case
Older than 70 million years, younger than 66
Anywhere between 66 and 70 million years old
Between 66 and 70 thousand years of age
questions.why: Bracketing gives a range, not a point: the fossil is younger than 70 Ma and older than 66 Ma.

questions.stem: How many years are in one million years?
options: One hundred thousand years, written 10 to the fifth
One billion years, written 10 to the ninth
One thousand years, written 10 to the third
One thousand thousand years, written 10 to the sixth
questions.why: A million is a thousand thousands, which is the unit used in plate-rate arithmetic.

questions.stem: Why can sedimentary rock usually not be dated directly by radiometric methods?
options: Its grains formed earlier, so dates mix source ages
Its minerals contain almost no radioactive isotopes at all
Its layers form too quickly to accumulate daughter atoms
Its half-life changes when the sediment gets compacted
questions.why: Sedimentary grains are recycled from older rocks, so a whole-rock date averages unrelated source ages.

questions.stem: Mars is smaller than Earth and shows little plate motion today. What best explains that?
options: A smaller planet retains much more radiogenic heat than Earth
A smaller planet cooled off much faster, weakening mantle convection
A smaller planet has a thicker mantle that convects faster
A smaller planet has no core to generate any heat
questions.why: Surface-area-to-volume ratio is higher on small bodies, so they lose heat and shut down convection sooner.

questions.stem: Early Earth had more short-lived radioactive isotopes. What followed for its interior?
options: Slower convection and a completely static lithosphere
A colder mantle with no plumes there
Faster convection and more vigorous tectonic activity
A liquid inner core and no field
questions.why: More decay heat early on drove stronger convection, which is why ancient crust records intense tectonic activity.

questions.stem: Which statement is an example of relative dating only?
options: Fossil A is exactly 250 million years old today
Fossil A contains 12.5 percent of the parent isotope
Fossil A has a half-life of 700 million years
Fossil A lies in a layer below fossil B
questions.why: Relative dating gives order, not a number in years.

questions.stem: Which statement is an example of absolute dating?
options: The ash layer is 66 million years old
The ash layer is older than the limestone
The ash layer sits beneath the sandstone
The ash layer cuts across a folded shale
questions.why: Absolute dating gives an age in years, which is what a radiometric result provides.

questions.stem: A dike cuts across three sedimentary layers. Which is youngest?
options: The lowest layer, because superposition always applies here
The dike, because it cuts the other units
The top layer, because it sits above the others
All three layers, because they all formed together
questions.why: Cross-cutting: the feature doing the cutting is younger than everything it cuts.

questions.stem: How do index fossils help correlate rock layers?
options: They give an absolute age measured in years
They show which layer was later metamorphosed
They identify layers of the same relative age
They prove the layers were never intensely folded
questions.why: Index fossils are short-lived species with wide distribution, so their presence marks a relative age.

questions.stem: Why does a half-life not depend on temperature or pressure?
options: Decay is a chemical process, sped up by heat
Decay is a mechanical process, slowed by pressure
Decay is a surface process, changed by erosion
Decay is a nuclear process, unaffected by surroundings
questions.why: Radioactive decay happens in the nucleus, where ordinary temperature and pressure changes have no effect.

questions.stem: A sample shows 87.5 percent daughter isotope. How many half-lives have passed?
options: Three, because 12.5 percent of the parent remains
Two, because 25 percent of the parent remains
One, because 50 percent of the parent remains
Four, because 6.25 percent of the parent remains
questions.why: Daughter at 87.5 percent leaves parent at 12.5 percent, which is three halvings.

questions.stem: Which isotope would you choose for a 100-million-year-old volcanic rock?
options: Carbon-14, whose half-life suits that age range
Potassium-40, whose half-life suits that age range
Uranium-238, whose half-life is too long to resolve
Nitrogen-14, which does not occur in volcanic rock
questions.why: K-40's 1.25-billion-year half-life leaves measurable parent and daughter at 100 Ma.

questions.stem: Which statement about Earth's present-day heat budget is correct?
options: Almost none of surface heat flow is radiogenic today
All of the surface heat flow comes from the Sun
Roughly half of surface heat flow is radiogenic today
Heat flow is highest in continental interiors right now
questions.why: Radiogenic decay supplies about half of the heat leaving the surface, with the rest draining primordial heat.

questions.stem: Two rocks carry the same isotope; one shows 25 percent parent, the other 50 percent. Which is older?
options: The 50 percent sample, having lost only two half-lives
Both samples are the same age, having lost one
Neither sample can be dated with that isotope here
The 25 percent sample, having lost two half-lives
questions.why: Less parent means more elapsed time, so 25 percent is two half-lives and older than the 50 percent sample.

questions.stem: What is the main limitation of a labeled cross-section model of Earth?
options: It is a two-dimensional snapshot that is not to scale
It cannot show all four layers at the same time
It cannot include either temperature or any depth information
It will necessarily mislabel both the crust and the mantle
questions.why: A cross-section is a static 2D diagram; adding scale bars, temperatures and arrows is what makes it quantitative.

questions.stem: What must a free body diagram show?
options: One isolated object and every force on it
One isolated object and every force it applies
Every object in the scene and all their forces
One moving object plus arrows showing its velocity
questions.why: An FBD isolates a single object and lists only the external forces acting on that object.

questions.stem: Which item is never drawn on a free body diagram?
options: A weight arrow that points straight downward
A velocity arrow showing the object's motion
A normal force arrow perpendicular to a surface
A friction arrow pointing against the motion
questions.why: Velocity is not a force; drawing it is the most common way to lose marks on this item.

questions.stem: A block rests on a ramp tilted at an angle. Which arrow points straight down?
options: Normal force, which acts perpendicular to the ramp surface
Friction, which acts parallel to the ramp surface
Weight, which always acts vertically toward Earth's center
The applied push, which acts along the ramp surface
questions.why: Weight is always vertical regardless of the surface; only normal force tilts with the ramp.

questions.stem: How is the normal force drawn on a free body diagram?
options: Parallel to the surface, pointing along the motion
Straight down, parallel to the object's weight
Opposite the applied force, whatever its direction
Perpendicular to the surface, pointing away from it
questions.why: Normal force is a contact push from the surface, so it is perpendicular and outward.

questions.stem: How is friction drawn on a free body diagram?
options: Along the surface, opposing the object's motion
Perpendicular to the surface, pointing away from it
Straight down, parallel to the object's weight
Along the surface, pointing with the object's motion
questions.why: Friction resists sliding, so its arrow runs along the surface against the motion.

questions.stem: On a plate free body diagram, which arrow should be drawn longest?
options: Ridge push, pointing outward away from the spreading ridge
Slab pull, pointing down and inward at the trench
Friction, pointing back along the plate's base and sides
Mantle drag, pointing along the base with the flow
questions.why: Slab pull is the dominant plate force, so it takes the longest arrow in the diagram.

questions.stem: In which direction does the slab pull arrow point on a plate diagram?
options: Upward and outward, away from the sinking slab
Sideways along the ridge, parallel to the boundary
Downward and inward, following the cold sinking slab
Straight upward, directly opposite the plate's weight vector
questions.why: The dense slab sinks, so it pulls the plate down and inward toward the mantle.

questions.stem: In which direction does the ridge push arrow point on a plate diagram?
options: Inward and up-slope, toward the elevated ridge crest
Straight downward, parallel to the plate's own weight
Along the ridge axis, parallel to the spreading center
Outward and down-slope, away from the elevated ridge
questions.why: The ridge stands high, so lithosphere slides away from it downhill: outward and down-slope.

questions.stem: In which direction does the mantle drag arrow point on a plate diagram?
options: Along the plate's base, in the direction of mantle flow
Across the plate's base, perpendicular to the mantle flow there
Straight down into the mantle layer beneath the plate edge
Along the plate's base, opposite the direction of the flow
questions.why: Mantle drag is the friction-like coupling to flow beneath the plate, so it follows the flow.

questions.stem: A plate moves at constant speed. What do the arrows in its diagram show?
options: Driving arrows are longer than all resisting arrows
Driving and resisting arrows are equal in length
Resisting arrows are longer than all driving arrows
No arrows are needed because the plate is moving
questions.why: Constant speed means zero net force, so the forward and backward arrows match.

questions.stem: How is an accelerating object shown in a free body diagram?
options: All arrows are equal, giving zero net force overall
A velocity arrow is added beside the force arrows
One direction's arrows are longer, giving a net force
The arrows are replaced by a single motion arrow
questions.why: Unbalanced arrows mean net force, and net force means acceleration in that direction.

questions.stem: Which label correctly names an object's weight on a diagram?
options: F with a subscript N, equal to mass times gravity
F with a subscript f, equal to mass times gravity
F with a subscript T, equal to mass times gravity
F with a subscript g, equal to mass times gravity
questions.why: Weight is F_g, or mg; F_N is normal force, f is friction, and T is tension.

questions.stem: An arrow along a plate's base is unlabeled and points against the motion. What is it?
options: Friction, which resists sliding along the base
Slab pull, which accelerates the plate downward
Ridge push, which drives the plate outward
Mantle drag, which carries the plate along
questions.why: The arrow opposing motion along a surface is friction, so it needs the label f.

questions.stem: Why are reaction forces left off a free body diagram?
options: They always cancel, so they can never matter
They act on other objects, not on this object
They are smaller, so they can be safely ignored
They act only after the object starts moving
questions.why: An FBD lists forces on the chosen object; the forces it exerts elsewhere belong to other diagrams.

questions.stem: A mass hangs at rest from a single rope. What does its diagram show?
options: Tension down and weight up, equal in length
Tension up and weight down, weight much longer
Tension up and weight down, equal in length
Only tension, because a hanging mass has no weight
questions.why: At rest the forces balance, so tension equals weight and the arrows match.

questions.stem: A crate slides across a level floor as you push it. Which pair opposes each other?
options: The weight downward and the friction backward
The normal force up and the applied push
The weight downward and the push forward
The push forward and the friction backward
questions.why: Along the direction of motion, the applied push and friction are the opposing pair.

questions.stem: On a ramp, which force has a component pointing down the slope?
options: Weight, whose component along the slope pulls downhill
Normal force, whose component along the slope pulls downhill
Friction, whose component along the slope pulls downhill
The normal force and friction together, pulling downhill
questions.why: Weight is vertical, so on a tilted surface part of it points down the slope.

questions.stem: Two horizontal forces act: 10 newtons right and 10 newtons left. What is the motion?
options: Constant acceleration to the right, since 10 newtons
No acceleration, because the net force is zero
Constant acceleration to the left, since 10 newtons
Undefined, because equal forces cannot be drawn
questions.why: Equal and opposite forces give zero net force, so there is no acceleration.

questions.stem: Which vertical pair belongs on a plate diagram when balance is asked for?
options: Weight down and slab pull up from the descending end
Ridge push down and mantle drag up under the plate
Weight down and buoyant support up from the asthenosphere
Friction down and normal force up at the plate edge
questions.why: Vertically, the plate's weight is matched by buoyant support from the mantle beneath.

questions.stem: Which mistake costs the most marks on a diagram?
options: Arrows drawn slightly shorter than all of the others
The object drawn as a box, not a circle
The diagram drawn without a title or caption
All of the arrows drawn correctly but left unlabeled
questions.why: Rubrics award the labels: an unlabeled arrow cannot be credited as a force.

questions.stem: A plate diagram shows equal opposing arrows. What does that establish?
options: The plate moves at a steady speed, not accelerating
The plate is still accelerating toward the trench quickly
The plate is not moving in any direction whatsoever
The plate has no forces acting on it whatsoever
questions.why: Balanced arrows mean zero net force, which with motion means constant velocity.

questions.stem: Which two arrows should point in roughly opposite directions?
options: Weight downward and ridge push outward along the plate
Ridge push outward, slab pull inward along the plate
Mantle drag and slab pull, both pointing inward there
Friction and mantle drag, both pointing with the flow
questions.why: The along-plate pair is drive and resistance: ridge push one way, slab pull the other.

questions.stem: Which pair correctly sorts these forces by type?
options: Friction acts at a distance; weight is contact
Both friction and weight are contact forces
Friction is contact; weight acts at a distance
Both friction and weight act at a distance
questions.why: Contact forces need touching surfaces; weight is the long-range gravitational pull.

questions.stem: Why is slab pull stronger than ridge push?
options: A ridge stands higher, so it pushes harder
Ridge push acts on a much larger plate area
Slab pull only acts after the plate stops moving
A cold dense slab sinks under its own weight
questions.why: The sinking slab's gravitational pull exceeds the push from the elevated ridge.

questions.stem: Which statement about ridges and slabs is correct?
options: Ridges push plates apart; slabs pull plates inward
Ridges pull plates together; slabs push plates apart
Ridges pull plates apart; slabs also pull plates apart
Ridges push plates apart; slabs push plates outward
questions.why: Only slabs pull; ridges push. Reversing that is the commonest plate-force error.

questions.stem: At an ocean-continent convergent boundary, which plate subducts?
options: The continental plate, because it is denser there
The oceanic plate, because it is denser there
Neither plate, because both are equally dense there
Whichever plate is moving faster at that boundary
questions.why: Density decides: old oceanic lithosphere sinks beneath lighter continental crust.

questions.stem: What happens to crust at a trench?
options: Young crust is created as magma rises
Crust is neither created nor destroyed there
Old crust is destroyed as it sinks
Crust is pushed sideways without changing age
questions.why: Trenches consume old cold crust; ridges create young hot crust.

questions.stem: Why does a transform boundary produce no volcanoes?
options: Magma forms but cools before reaching the surface
The crust there is far too thick to melt
Volcanoes do form there, but only under water
Nothing rises or subducts, so no magma forms
questions.why: Melting requires decompression or added water, and transform motion supplies neither.

questions.stem: Symmetric magnetic stripes on the seafloor are evidence for what?
options: New crust forming and spreading away from a ridge
Old crust being compressed and folded at a ridge
A stationary ridge sitting on older unmoving seafloor rock
Deep sediment layers aligning with the present magnetic field
questions.why: Each reversal is recorded on both sides, so the pattern mirrors as crust spreads.

questions.stem: Why is heat flow highest at a mid-ocean ridge?
options: Old crust there is still slowly heating up
New crust there is still hot and cooling
Friction along the ridge generates the extra heat
Thick sediment traps heat at the ridge axis
questions.why: Young crust near the ridge has not cooled yet, so heat flow is high there.

questions.stem: Which statement separates relative from absolute dating?
options: Relative gives years; absolute gives only the order
Relative uses isotopes; absolute uses layer superposition
Relative gives order; absolute gives ages in years
Relative dates single minerals; absolute dates whole rocks
questions.why: Relative dating orders events; radiometric methods return a number in years.

questions.stem: Which isotope dates a 100-million-year-old volcanic rock?
options: Carbon-14, whose half-life fits that span
Uranium-238, whose half-life is far too long
Nitrogen-14, which volcanic rock does not contain
Potassium-40, whose half-life fits that span
questions.why: K-40's 1.25-billion-year half-life leaves measurable parent and daughter at 100 Ma.

questions.stem: Roughly how long is carbon-14 useful for dating?
options: About 50,000 years, or nine to ten half-lives
About 5,000 years, or one single half-life
About 50 million years, or nine thousand half-lives
About 5 million years, or nine hundred half-lives
questions.why: Past about ten half-lives too little parent remains, so C-14 stops near 50,000 years.

questions.stem: A plate moves 5 cm per year. How far does it move in 10 million years?
options: 500 km, since 5 cm per year is 50 km per million
50 km, since 5 cm per year is 5 km per million
5,000 km, since 5 cm per year is 500 km per million
100 km, since 5 cm per year is 10 km per million
questions.why: 1 cm/yr is 10 km/My, so 5 cm/yr is 50 km/My and 10 My gives 500 km.

questions.stem: A plate moves 2 cm per year. How far does it move in 30 million years?
options: 60 km, since 2 cm per year is 2 km per million
600 km, since 2 cm per year is 20 km per million
3,000 km, since 2 cm per year is 100 km per million
12,000 km, since 2 cm per year is 400 km per million
questions.why: 2 cm/yr equals 20 km/My, and 20 km/My over 30 My is 600 km.

questions.stem: Three half-lives of a 400-million-year isotope have passed. What is the age, and how much parent remains?
options: 800 million years, with 12.5 percent parent left
1.2 billion years, with 25 percent parent left
1.2 billion years, with 12.5 percent parent left
400 million years, with 12.5 percent parent left
questions.why: Three half-lives times 400 My is 1.2 By, and three halvings leave 12.5 percent parent.

questions.stem: A rock holds 6.25 percent parent and the half-life is 1 billion years. How old is it?
options: 2 billion years, since two half-lives elapsed
3 billion years, since three half-lives elapsed
6 billion years, since six half-lives elapsed
4 billion years, since four half-lives elapsed
questions.why: 100 to 50 to 25 to 12.5 to 6.25 percent is four halvings, so 4 times 1 By is 4 By.

questions.stem: What parent-to-daughter ratio appears after exactly one half-life?
options: 1 to 1, since half the parent has decayed
1 to 3, since a quarter of the parent remains
1 to 7, since an eighth of the parent remains
1 to 15, since a sixteenth of the parent remains
questions.why: After one half-life, half the parent has become daughter, so the ratio is 1:1.

questions.stem: A sample shows a parent-to-daughter ratio of 1 to 15. How many half-lives have passed?
options: Three, since only 12.5 percent parent remains
Four, since only 6.25 percent parent remains
Two, since only 25 percent parent remains
Five, since only 3.125 percent parent remains
questions.why: A 1:15 ratio leaves 6.25 percent parent, which is four halvings.

questions.stem: A sample holds one-sixteenth of its original parent isotope. How many half-lives passed?
options: Three, because the parent halved three separate times
Five, because the parent halved five separate times
Four, because the parent halved four separate times
Two, because the parent halved two separate times
questions.why: One-sixteenth is 6.25 percent, which is four halvings of the original amount.

questions.stem: Which isotope suits a 2-billion-year-old granitic rock?
options: Carbon-14, whose half-life fits only thousands of years
Potassium-40, whose half-life fits only millions of years
Radon-222, whose half-life fits only several days
Uranium-238, whose half-life fits many billions of years
questions.why: U-238's 4.5-billion-year half-life leaves measurable parent and daughter at 2 By.

questions.stem: Which isotope suits a 30,000-year-old bone fragment?
options: Carbon-14, whose half-life fits tens of thousands of years
Uranium-238, whose half-life fits several billions of years
Rubidium-87, whose half-life fits tens of billions of years
Potassium-40, whose half-life fits about a billion years there
questions.why: A 5,730-year half-life means measurable parent remains at 30,000 years, about five half-lives.

questions.stem: Which equation gives the age of a sample once half-lives are counted?
options: Age equals the half-life divided by number of half-lives
Age equals the number of half-lives times the half-life
Age equals the percentage of parent times the half-life
Age equals the daughter percentage times the parent count
questions.why: Counting halvings gives n, and multiplying n by the isotope's half-life gives the age.

questions.stem: A parent-remaining curve falls from 100 to 50 to 25 percent. What does each drop show?
options: Two half-lives passing, measured along the time axis
One daughter isotope escaping from the mineral grain
One half-life passing, measured along the time axis
A single mineral grain starting to crystallize slowly
questions.why: The curve is exponential, so every halving of the y-value is one half-life on the x-axis.

questions.stem: What does a reliable radiometric date require of the mineral?
options: An open system, with daughter atoms escaping out steadily
A melted state, so parent and daughter can mix
A heated state, so the ratio can reset completely
A closed system, with no parent or daughter escaping
questions.why: Gain or loss of either isotope breaks the ratio, so the mineral must stay closed.

questions.stem: In an undisturbed sequence, which layer is oldest?
options: The bottom layer, by the principle of superposition
The top layer, by the principle of superposition
The middle layer, because it is squeezed hardest
All layers are the same age in undisturbed rock
questions.why: Superposition: undisturbed layers stack with the oldest at the base.

questions.stem: What does an unconformity record in a sequence?
options: A single layer that formed unusually quickly
A gap in time from erosion or non-deposition
A fault that shifted layers sideways later
A fold that inverted the whole sequence
questions.why: An unconformity is missing time: material was eroded or never deposited.

questions.stem: A sandstone contains a pebble of granite. Which is older?
options: The sandstone, which formed before the granite pebble
Both formed at the same time in one event
The granite pebble, which formed before the sandstone
The order cannot be determined from one pebble
questions.why: The inclusion principle: a clast must exist before the rock that contains it.

questions.stem: How are index fossils used in a rock sequence?
options: To measure the absolute age in millions of years
To show that no folding ever affected the layers
To prove the sediment was never deposited in water
To identify layers of the same relative age
questions.why: Index fossils are short-lived, wide-ranging species, so they correlate relative age.

questions.stem: A fault offsets four layers. What is its age relative to them?
options: Younger than the layers it offsets
Older than the layers it offsets
Same age as the lowest layer
Impossible to place without radiometric dating
questions.why: Cross-cutting: whatever does the cutting is younger than what it cuts.

questions.stem: A fossil lies between ash dated 80 Ma and ash dated 74 Ma. What is its age?
options: Exactly 77 million years old in every case
Anywhere between 74 and 80 million years old
Older than 80 million years, younger than 74
Between 74 and 80 thousand years of age
questions.why: Bracketing gives a range: younger than 80 Ma, older than 74 Ma.

questions.stem: Why is no ocean crust older than about 200 million years?
options: Ocean crust forms too slowly to reach older ages
Ocean crust is melted away by ridge volcanism only
Ocean crust is destroyed at trenches by subduction
Ocean crust is buried by sediment before it ages
questions.why: Oceanic lithosphere recycles into the mantle, so seafloor is geologically young.

questions.stem: Where in an ocean basin is the crust oldest?
options: At the ridge axis, where crust is newest
Midway between the ridge and the trench
Directly beneath the continental shelf edge there
Farthest from the ridge, nearest the trench
questions.why: Crust ages with distance from the spreading center, so the oldest lies near trenches.

questions.stem: What does a mirrored magnetic stripe pattern across a ridge indicate?
options: Crust formed at the ridge and moved outward both ways
Crust formed at both edges and moved toward the ridge
The ridge axis migrated slowly while the crust stayed fixed
Magnetic minerals settled from the ocean water in stripes
questions.why: Symmetry means both sides left the same axis, which is spreading.

questions.stem: GPS vectors at a divergent boundary point in which directions?
options: Toward the boundary from both sides here
Away from the boundary on both sides
Same direction on both sides of the boundary
Vertically downward into the mantle on both sides
questions.why: Divergence means the plates separate, so each vector points away from the boundary.

questions.stem: How does heat flow change across an ocean basin?
options: It is lowest at the ridge and rises with crust age
It is uniform across the whole basin at all ages
It is highest at the ridge and falls with crust age
It is highest at the trench and lowest at the ridge
questions.why: Young hot crust near the ridge loses heat fastest, so measured flow is highest there.

questions.stem: Why does one plate descend at an ocean-continent boundary?
options: The continental plate is denser than the oceanic plate
The oceanic plate is much thicker and therefore heavier
The continental plate moves faster and pushes it down
The oceanic plate is denser than the mantle beneath
questions.why: Old cold oceanic lithosphere is dense enough to sink; continental crust is buoyant.

questions.stem: How do earthquake depths reveal a subducting slab?
options: Depth increases inland, following the dipping cold slab
Depth decreases inland, following the rising hot mantle
Depth stays shallow and constant across the margin
Depth is deepest at the ridge and trench
questions.why: The Benioff zone tracks the slab, so quakes deepen away from the trench.

questions.stem: Which set of observations identifies a transform boundary?
options: Deep quakes, a trench, and explosive volcanoes
Shallow quakes, offset rock units, and no volcanoes
Shallow quakes, new crust, and high heat flow
Intermediate quakes, folded rock, and thick crust
questions.why: Lateral slip produces shallow quakes and offsets, with no magma generated.

questions.stem: What forms when two continental plates collide?
options: A trench with deep quakes and island arcs
A ridge with new crust and shallow quakes
A mountain belt with thickened crust, no trench
A transform fault with offset stream channels there
questions.why: Neither continent subducts easily, so the crust shortens and thickens instead.

questions.stem: Why does melting occur beneath a mid-ocean ridge?
options: Water from the slab lowers the rock's melting point
Friction between the separating plates generates the magma
Compression at the ridge squeezes rock into liquid
Rising mantle decompresses, sharply lowering its melting point
questions.why: Decompression melting as mantle rises feeds the ridge; water-driven melting belongs to subduction.

questions.stem: Which pair correctly distinguishes Earth's two heat sources?
options: Primordial is leftover; radiogenic is produced now
Primordial is produced now; radiogenic is leftover
Primordial comes from the Sun; radiogenic from friction
Primordial comes from tides; radiogenic from pressure
questions.why: Accretional heat still draining out is primordial; decay heat is generated continuously.

questions.stem: What does the S-wave shadow zone prove about the outer core?
options: It is solid, because shear waves speed up inside it
It is liquid, because shear waves cannot cross it
It is empty, because no waves reach that region
It is denser than the inner core beneath it
questions.why: S-waves require a solid, so their absence beyond the shadow is evidence of liquid.

questions.stem: Why is the inner core solid while the outer core is liquid?
options: The inner core contains no iron to melt
The inner core is cooler than outer core rock
Pressure at that depth raises the melting point
Convection keeps the inner core from ever melting
questions.why: Higher pressure raises the melting point, so the deepest iron solidifies despite being hotter.

questions.stem: Mars shows little plate motion today. What best accounts for that?
options: A smaller planet kept more radiogenic heat inside
A smaller planet has a mantle that convects faster
A smaller planet never had any radioactive isotopes
A smaller planet lost heat faster, weakening convection
questions.why: Small bodies have more surface per volume, so they cool and shut down convection sooner.

questions.stem: Early Earth held more short-lived isotopes. What followed inside it?
options: Stronger convection and much more vigorous tectonics
Weaker convection and a completely static crust
A colder mantle with no plumes anywhere
A liquid inner core with no field
questions.why: More decay heat meant stronger convection, which is why ancient crust records intense activity.
